title: Find a probability with equally likely outcomes
show: 6 by 6 grid of two-dice sums with the sums of 9 or more highlighted

example.question: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores are added. Find the probability that the sum is $9$ or more.

steps.say: Each die has $6$ faces and any face can go with any face. Multiply to get the total number of outcomes.
List the pairs that give a sum of $9$ or more. Count how many pairs give each sum.
Divide the $\hl{1}{10}$ favourable outcomes by the $\hl{2}{36}$ possible outcomes. Cancel to simplest form.

title: Use set notation and Venn diagrams for probability
show: Venn diagram of 40 students: drama only 12, both 6, choir only 8, neither 14

example.question: In a class of $40$ students, $18$ take drama and $14$ take choir. $6$ students take both. A student is picked at random. Find the probability that the student takes neither drama nor choir.

steps.say: Write $\hl{1}{6}$ in the part where the circles overlap. Subtract it from each circle to get the parts with one subject only.
Add the three parts inside the circles. This is everyone who takes at least one subject.
Everyone not in a circle takes neither. Subtract from the total of $40$.
Put the $\hl{2}{14}$ students over the $40$ in the class and cancel.

title: Apply the addition rule
show: Venn diagram of A and B with the regions filled in from P(A), P(B), P(A∪B)

example.question: $A$ and $B$ are events with $P(A) = \frac{3}{5}$, $P(B) = \frac{3}{10}$ and $P(A \cup B) = \frac{7}{10}$. Find $P(A \cap B)$. Hence state whether $A$ and $B$ are independent.
example.final: P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{5}, \text{ so } A \text{ and } B \text{ are not independent}

steps.say: Start with the rule for $A$ or $B$. It has $P(A \cap B)$ in it, and that is what we want.
Put the numbers in and make $\hl{1}{P(A \cap B)}$ the subject.
Independent events satisfy $P(A) \times P(B) = P(A \cap B)$. Multiply $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ and compare with $\hl{1}{\frac{1}{5}}$.
Compare the two values.

rows.aside: They are not equal, so $A$ and $B$ are **not independent**.

title: Use a tree diagram for multi-stage experiments
show: probability tree for two kicks, each branch scores 7/10 or misses 3/10

example.question: Sam takes two penalty kicks. The probability that he scores any one kick is $\frac{7}{10}$. Draw a tree diagram and find the probability that he scores at least one of the two kicks.

steps.say: Each kick has two branches: score ($S$) with $\frac{7}{10}$ and miss ($M$) with $\frac{3}{10}$. Both first-kick branches split again for the second kick.

rows.aside: Second kick: the same two branches from each of those.

steps.say: The probability of one outcome is the product of the numbers along its branches.
At least one score means $S,S$ or $S,M$ or $M,S$. Add those three outcomes.
The only way to score none is $M,M$. Take $\hl{2}{\frac{9}{100}}$ away from $1$.

title: Test whether events are independent
show: Venn diagram of A and B with P(A)=0.5, P(A∩B)=0.1, P(A∪B)=0.7 filled in

example.question: $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. Find $P(B)$. Hence decide whether $A$ and $B$ are independent events.
example.final: P(B) = 0.3 \text{ and } P(A)P(B) = 0.15 \neq 0.1 = P(A \cap B) \text{: not independent}

steps.say: Use the addition rule, $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$, and solve for $P(B)$.
Independent events satisfy $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$. Work out the product $\hl{1}{P(A)P(B)}$.
Compare the product with $\hl{2}{P(A \cap B)}$, which the question gives as $0.1$.

rows.aside: The product and $P(A \cap B)$ are not equal. So the events are **not independent**. Always write that sentence.

title: Apply conditional probability and the general multiplication rule
show: Venn diagram or tree with bike 60%, bike and car 24%

example.question: In a survey, $60\%$ of people own a bike. $24\%$ own a bike and a car. A person who owns a bike is chosen at random. Find the probability that this person owns a car.

steps.say: Let $B$ be owning a bike and $C$ be owning a car. We are **told** the person owns a bike, so the bike is the condition.

rows.aside: We want $P(C \mid B)$, the chance of a car given a bike.

steps.say: The overlap goes on top. The thing we are told, $\hl{2}{P(B)}$, goes on the bottom.

rows.aside: This is not $P(B \mid C)$. That would divide by $P(C)$.

steps.say: Put in the two numbers and divide.
